summary.title: NUMA Memory Performance
summary.one_liner: Learn how Linux describes NUMA memory nodes by initiator-target access classes, rated bandwidth and latency in sysfs, and memory-side caches.
keywords: how to check numa latency and bandwidth
takeaways: Memory is grouped into NUMA nodes; initiators (CPUs or I/O devices) access memory targets, and each pair is ranked into access classes, with class 0 as the highest performing.
Kernel sysfs exports rated read/write bandwidth (MiB/s) and latency (ns) under nodeY/access0/initiators/, with access class 1 covering CPU-only initiators.
Memory-side caches are transparent to software; the kernel exposes their size, line size, indexing and write policy under memory_side_cache/ when firmware such as ACPI HMAT provides the data.
Near memory is the fastest cache level and far memory is the last-level memory the system addresses, which is numbered differently from CPU L1/L2/L3 caches.
summary.summary: This kernel documentation page explains NUMA memory performance in Linux. It covers how heterogeneous memory is grouped into nodes, how initiator-target pairs are ranked into access classes, and how the kernel exports rated bandwidth and latency through sysfs. It also describes memory-side caches, near and far memory terminology, and the cache attributes available under memory_side_cache, with ACPI HMAT cited as one discovery source.
